```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# gstat fits the variograms behind the design effect and the kriging check,
# and ggplot2 draws the two maps. Both are Suggests, so the chunks that use
# them are gated and the rest runs on the hard dependencies.
# `eval` gates chunks only: knitr does not apply it to inline `r ...` code,
# which runs regardless. An inline reference to something a gated chunk
# defines has to guard itself, or the article fails to build where the
# package is missing.
has_gstat  <- requireNamespace("gstat",   quietly = TRUE)
has_ggplot <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo      = TRUE,
  message   = FALSE,
  warning   = FALSE,
  fig.align = "center",
  out.width = "100%"
)
```

This article takes a layer of observations to cells. It chooses a
tessellation method, places the seeds of Voronoi cells, puts each observation
in a cell, and reads what `summarize_by_cell()` returns (the standard error
that fits the question, and the warnings about
[pooled values](glossary.html#pooled-value)). It also checks the cell mean
against block kriging with `kriging_adequacy()`. `vignette("resolution")` explains how to set
the number of cells, and `vignette("glossary")` defines the terms used here.

*This article needs two optional packages: `gstat` for the variograms behind
the design effect and the kriging check, and `ggplot2` for the maps. Where one
is missing, the code that needs it is shown but not run.*

## A simulated layer and its cell count

The layer is 350 points on a square 1,000 m on a side. The response `z` is 1.5
times a predictor `a`, plus a smooth spatial field and some noise; `b` is
noise alone.

```{r fixture}
library(sf)
library(spatialkit)

set.seed(11)
n  <- 350
xy <- data.frame(x = 5e5 + runif(n, 0, 1000), y = 5e6 + runif(n, 0, 1000))
D  <- as.matrix(dist(xy))
field <- as.numeric(t(chol(exp(-D / 70) + diag(1e-8, n))) %*% rnorm(n))
xy$a  <- rnorm(n)
xy$b  <- rnorm(n)
xy$z  <- 1.5 * xy$a + field + rnorm(n, sd = 0.3)
pts   <- st_as_sf(xy, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632)

prof <- resolution_profile(pts, "z")
size <- select_resolution(prof)
size$best
```

`resolution_profile()` and `select_resolution()`, at their defaults, size the
cells for pooled values at `r size$obs_per_cell_asked` observations per cell,
which gives `r size$best` cells for `r nrow(pts)` points.
`vignette("resolution")` explains the size and the other ways to set the
count.

## Choosing a tessellation method

`build_tessellation()` draws four kinds of cell.

- `"voronoi"` gives one cell per point it is given, each the part of the area
  nearer that point than any other. On the observations themselves that is
  one cell per observation, with no spread inside a cell to give a standard
  error. On seeds placed by `get_voronoi_seeds()` you set the count, and the
  cells follow the observations: small where they are dense, large where
  they are sparse.
- `"hex"` and `"square"` lay a grid of equal-area cells, clipped at the
  boundary, so you set the cell size and the data do not. Hexagons put all six neighbours of a cell at the
  same distance; squares line up with the axes of the CRS. A grid laid over
  the whole area can leave cells with no observation, more of them the more
  the points cluster.
- `"triangles"` returns the Delaunay triangulation of the points. It is for
  interpolation and work on adjacency, and is not meant as a cell to
  summarise in.

`"hex"` and `"square"` need a `boundary` to lay the grid over. `clip_target_for()`
returns one polygon to tessellate within: the bounding box of the points,
widened by `expand` (a fraction of its longer side below 1, a distance in CRS
units otherwise). Passing the same polygon to every method makes the
tessellations cover the same ground.

```{r methods}
bnd   <- clip_target_for(pts, expand = 0.02, quiet = TRUE)
seeds <- get_voronoi_seeds(n = size, sample_points = pts)

vor <- build_tessellation(seeds, boundary = bnd, method = "voronoi",
                          quiet = TRUE)
hex <- build_tessellation(pts, boundary = bnd, method = "hex",
                          approx_n_cells = size, quiet = TRUE)
sq  <- build_tessellation(pts, boundary = bnd, method = "square",
                          approx_n_cells = size, quiet = TRUE)

c(voronoi = nrow(vor$cells), hex = nrow(hex$cells), square = nrow(sq$cells))
```

```{r method-counts, include=FALSE}
# Points per cell under each method, for the figure and the sentence below.
per_cell <- function(cells, method) {
  ids <- assign_features_to_polygons(pts, cells, polygon_id_col = "cell_id",
                                     quiet = TRUE)$cell_id
  cells$n <- tabulate(match(ids, cells$cell_id), nrow(cells))
  cells$method <- method
  cells[, c("method", "n")]
}
three <- rbind(per_cell(vor$cells, "Voronoi on seeds"),
               per_cell(hex$cells, "hex"),
               per_cell(sq$cells,  "square"))
three$method <- factor(three$method, c("Voronoi on seeds", "hex", "square"))
empty <- tapply(three$n == 0, three$method, sum)
three$n[three$n == 0] <- NA
methods_alt <- sprintf(paste(
  "Three maps of the same square area, each cell shaded by the points it",
  "holds. Of the %d Voronoi cells on seeds, %s empty; the hex grid of",
  "%d cells has %d empty cells and the square grid of %d cells has %d,",
  "shown in grey."),
  nrow(vor$cells), if (empty[[1]] == 0) "none is" else paste(empty[[1]], "are"),
  nrow(hex$cells), empty[[2]],
  nrow(sq$cells), empty[[3]])
```

```{r methods-map, eval=has_ggplot, fig.height=2.6, fig.alt=methods_alt}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(three) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = n), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ method) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "points\nin cell", na.value = "grey85") +
  theme_void()
```

```{r methods-no-ggplot, echo=FALSE, eval=!has_ggplot, results='asis'}
cat("*(The map needs `ggplot2`, which is not installed here.)*\n")
```

Asked for the same count, the hex grid builds `r nrow(hex$cells)` cells,
`r empty[["hex"]]` of them with no observation, and the square grid
`r nrow(sq$cells)`, `r empty[["square"]]` empty, while the
`r nrow(vor$cells)` Voronoi cells on k-means seeds have
`r if (empty[[1]] == 0) "none" else empty[[1]]` empty. These points are
drawn uniformly over the square; on clustered points the grids leave more cells
empty. `?build_tessellation` gives the rules each method follows.

## Placing Voronoi seeds

`get_voronoi_seeds()` places the seeds three ways. `method = "kmeans"`, the
default, takes the centres of a k-means partition of `sample_points`;
`"random"` draws seeds uniformly inside `boundary`; `"provided"` takes the
seeds you pass.

Given the result of `select_resolution()` as `n`, as above, the k-means
method returns the centres of the partition the profile scored, so the
Voronoi cells are the cells the criteria judged and nothing is drawn at
random. Given a number, it runs a new k-means. Under the default
`partition = "density"` each point is weighted by its local density, which
gives many small cells where the points are dense and a few large ones where
they are sparse. Its draws come from the session's random-number stream: call
`set.seed()` first, or pass `set_seed`, to get the same seeds again. For
k-means, `n` is an upper bound, so check `nrow()` on the result.

```{r seeds}
nrow(seeds)   # the centres the profile scored
fresh <- get_voronoi_seeds(n = size$best, sample_points = pts, set_seed = 1)
nrow(fresh)   # a new density-weighted k-means
```

The seeds carry the hull of `sample_points` as their cover, so
`build_tessellation(seeds)` without a boundary still makes cells that hold
every observation. The seeds of `select_resolution()` also carry the record
of how the count was set, which the cells and the assigned rows keep (see
"Pooled values and their warnings" below).

## Putting each observation in a cell

`assign_features_to_polygons()` returns the observations, one row each, with
the ID of the cell that holds them.

```{r assign}
asg_v <- assign_features_to_polygons(pts, vor$cells, polygon_id_col = "cell_id")
head(asg_v$cell_id)
```

```{r assign-counts, include=FALSE}
n_v <- tabulate(match(asg_v$cell_id, vor$cells$cell_id), nrow(vor$cells))
```

The `r nrow(vor$cells)` cells hold from `r min(n_v)` to `r max(n_v)` points
each. A point outside every cell is dropped, with a warning of class
`spatialkit_unassigned` that gives the count; `keep_unassigned = TRUE` keeps
it with `NA` as its cell. A point on the edge two cells share goes to one of
them by `tie_break`. `polygon_id_col = "cell_id"` keeps the name the cells
carry, so the later calls take `id_col = "cell_id"`.

### Grouping a layer of polygons

`assign_features_to_polygons()` takes polygons as well as points. With
`largest = TRUE`, the default, each polygon goes to the cell it overlaps
most, so the result has one row per polygon. The example groups North
Carolina's counties, which ship with `sf`, into hexagonal cells laid over the
state outline.

```{r group}
nc <- st_read(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf"), quiet = TRUE)
counties <- ensure_projected(nc[, c("NAME", "BIR74", "SID74")])
state    <- st_union(counties)
nc_cells <- build_tessellation(coerce_to_points(counties), boundary = state,
                               method = "hex", approx_n_cells = 12,
                               quiet = TRUE)$cells

grouped <- assign_features_to_polygons(counties, nc_cells,
                                       polygon_id_col = "cell_id")
joined  <- st_join(counties, nc_cells)

c(counties = nrow(counties), grouped = nrow(grouped), joined = nrow(joined))
```

```{r group-used, include=FALSE}
used <- length(unique(stats::na.omit(grouped$cell_id)))
used <- if (used == nrow(nc_cells)) paste("all", used) else
  paste(used, "of the", nrow(nc_cells))
```

The `r nrow(counties)` counties come back as `r nrow(grouped)` rows, spread
over `r used` cells, from `r min(table(grouped$cell_id))` to
`r max(table(grouped$cell_id))` counties each. `sf::st_join()` on the same
layers returns `r nrow(joined)` rows, one for each county and cell that touch
or overlap, so a count per cell taken from it counts a county once in every
cell it reaches.

```{r group-alt, include=FALSE}
grouped$cell <- factor(grouped$cell_id)
group_alt <- sprintf(paste(
  "The %d North Carolina counties, each filled with the colour of the",
  "hexagonal cell it overlaps most, under the outlines of the %d cells",
  "drawn over the state."), nrow(grouped), nrow(nc_cells))
```

```{r group-map, eval=has_ggplot, fig.height=2.6, fig.alt=group_alt}
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = grouped, aes(fill = cell), colour = "grey40",
          linewidth = 0.1) +
  geom_sf(data = nc_cells, fill = NA, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = grDevices::hcl.colors(nlevels(grouped$cell),
                                                   "Set 3"),
                    guide = "none") +
  theme_void()
```

```{r group-no-ggplot, echo=FALSE, eval=!has_ggplot, results='asis'}
cat("*(The map needs `ggplot2`, which is not installed here.)*\n")
```

## What summarize_by_cell() returns

`summarize_by_cell()` reduces the assigned rows to one row per cell. Passing
`cells_sf` attaches the cells' geometry, so the result maps, and keeps the
cells that hold no observation.

```{r summarise}
vals <- summarize_by_cell(asg_v, "z", id_col = "cell_id", cells_sf = vor$cells)
names(vals)
round(st_drop_geometry(vals)[1:4, -1], 3)
```

The columns, in order:

- `cell_id`, and `n`, the observations in the cell. A cell with none has
  `n = NA`, and stays in the result, so a map shows where there is no data.
- `resp_mean_z`, the plain mean of the response. With `predictor_vars`, each
  predictor gets `pred_mean_<name>` and its own columns of the kinds below.
- `..sd_resp_z` and `..se_resp_z`, the standard deviation inside the cell and
  the standard error of its mean. A cell of one observation has a standard
  error of `NA`.
- `cell_weight`, the cell's effective sample size: its count of non-missing
  responses, divided by the [design effect](glossary.html#design-effect) when
  `deff` applies one. Pass it as
  the weights of a regression on cell values.
- `..pooled_resp_z`, the pooled value: the cell's mean pulled toward the mean
  of the observations in the 8 nearest cells (nearest by the centroid of their
  observations). That mean is the cell's target, `..pooled_target_resp_z`.
  The cell's own weight, `..pooled_w_resp_z`, is the share of the pooled
  value that is the cell's own mean, and it grows with the cell's count.
  `estimate = "mean"` leaves these three columns out.

The plain mean and the pooled value both estimate the
[cell's true mean](glossary.html#cells-true-mean): the
expected value of one further observation located in the cell the way its
observations were. Neither is the average of a surface over the cell's area.
Pooled values are for maps and for predicting observations. For a regression
on cell values use the plain means with `cell_weight`; `..pooled_w_resp_z` is
not a regression weight.

Other arguments add columns. `deff` other than 1 adds `deff_applied` and
`deff_method`, `area = TRUE` adds `cell_area` and `n_per_area`, `conf_level`
adds a confidence interval for each mean (`..ci_lo_*`, `..ci_hi_*`), and
`obs_level` adds a range for one further observation in the cell around the
pooled value (`..obs_lo_*`, `..obs_hi_*`). Away from the observations no
interval here is calibrated. `vignette("reporting")` says which interval
answers which question, and `?summarize_by_cell` lists the columns under
"Output columns" and "Value".

## Standard errors and the design effect

The naive standard error of a cell mean, \(s/\sqrt{n}\), treats the points in
a cell as independent. As an estimate of the population (grand) mean, a cell
mean on an autocorrelated field varies more than that: the points in a cell
share the cell's departure from the population mean, so they carry less
information than their count.

The design effect is how many times larger a cell mean's variance is than
\(s^2/n\) says, and \(n/\text{deff}\) is the effective sample size. A
design effect estimated from the data (`"kish"` or `"variogram"`) also
corrects \(s\), which the same correlation biases low, so the standard error
comes out more than \(\sqrt{\text{deff}}\) times the naive one;
"Standard errors and design effects" in `?summarize_by_cell` gives the
formula. Leave
`deff = 1` when the cell means describe the cells, as on a map or in a
regression on cell values, and the points are spread through each cell. Set
`deff` when the cell means feed a claim about the whole population.

Kish's design effect, \(1 + (n - 1)\rho\) with \(\rho\) the intra-class
correlation inside a cell, grows with the count in a cell, so this section
uses bigger cells, from a square grid asked for 24.

```{r se-cells}
tess <- build_tessellation(pts, boundary = bnd, method = "square",
                           approx_n_cells = 24, quiet = TRUE)
asg  <- assign_features_to_polygons(pts, tess$cells)

c(cells = nrow(tess$cells), points = nrow(asg),
  median_per_cell = median(table(asg$poly_id)))
```

`summarize_by_cell()` takes the design effect as `deff`. Three settings on the
same cells:

```{r deff, eval=has_gstat}
sac  <- estimate_sac_range(pts, "z")
iid  <- summarize_by_cell(asg, "z", cells_sf = tess$cells, deff = 1)
kish <- summarize_by_cell(asg, "z", cells_sf = tess$cells, deff = "kish")
vgm  <- summarize_by_cell(asg, "z", cells_sf = tess$cells, deff = "variogram",
                          sac = sac)

data.frame(n         = iid$n,
           iid       = round(iid$..se_resp_z, 3),
           kish      = round(kish$..se_resp_z, 3),
           variogram = round(vgm$..se_resp_z, 3))[1:5, ]
```

```{r deff-inflation, echo=FALSE, results='asis', eval=has_gstat}
ik <- median(kish$..se_resp_z / iid$..se_resp_z, na.rm = TRUE)
iv <- median(vgm$..se_resp_z  / iid$..se_resp_z, na.rm = TRUE)
cat(sprintf(paste(
  "Across cells the standard error is a median %.2f times the naive one",
  "under `kish` and %.2f times under `variogram`. As an estimate of the population",
  "mean, a confidence interval built on the naive standard error is about",
  "%.0f percent of the width the variogram correction gives it on this",
  "field. For the cell's own mean the naive standard error is the better of",
  "the two, and close to right when the points are spread through the cell;",
  "the next section (`kriging_adequacy()`) measures how close on this",
  "field.\n"), ik, iv, 100 / iv))
```

```{r deff-no-gstat, echo=FALSE, eval=!has_gstat, results='asis'}
cat("*(This comparison needs `gstat`, which is not installed here.)*\n")
```

`deff = "kish"` estimates an intra-class correlation from the variance within
and between cells and applies Kish's factor. `deff = "variogram"` takes the
correlation from the fitted variogram, so it uses the spatial structure and
not the cell labels. When no usable variogram exists, that request falls back
to `"kish"` with a warning of class `spatialkit_deff_fallback`, and the
`deff_method` column names the correction each row carries. The result
records the correction and the per-cell design effects, and the Kish result
the intra-class correlation it used:

```{r deff-attrs, eval=has_gstat}
attr(vgm, "deff_applied")$method
summary(attr(vgm, "deff_applied")$deff)
attr(kish, "icc")$resp
```

A cell whose design effect reaches its count holds one observation's worth of
information, so its standard deviation says nothing about the spread and its
standard error is `NA`. Use bigger cells or collect more points.

## Is the cell mean the best estimate of the cell?

The plain mean weights every point in a cell equally and ignores everything
outside it. Block kriging weights the observations by their correlation with
the cell under a fitted variogram, borrows from neighbouring cells, and gives
a variance from the same model. `kriging_adequacy()` computes both for every
cell, without changing any cell value, and scores the variogram by blocked
cross-validation.

```{r kriging, eval=has_gstat}
ka <- kriging_adequacy(asg, "z", tess$cells, k = 4, seed = 1)
ka
```

`plain_var` is the error variance of the plain mean under the fitted
variogram. A naive `se^2` below it says the naive standard error is too small,
if the variogram is right. `kr_gain` is the share of that variance kriging
removes in the cell. `kr_ratio` is the kriging variance as a share of the
variance the cell mean has with no data, so 1 means the data say nothing
about the cell. `kr_shift` is how far the kriged estimate moved from the plain
mean, over the standard deviation the variogram gives that difference: about
a third of cells beyond 1 and one in twenty beyond 2 is what a right
variogram produces, and more says the means and the model disagree. The
blocked cross-validation at the end standardises each held-out error by its
kriging standard deviation: a variance of 1 for those standardised errors
means the kriging variance is right, and above 1 means it is too small.

```{r kriging-cols, eval=has_gstat}
round(as.data.frame(st_drop_geometry(ka))[1:4, c("n", "mean", "se",
                                                 "plain_var", "kr_pred",
                                                 "kr_var", "kr_ratio",
                                                 "kr_gain", "kr_shift")], 3)
```

```{r kriging-reading, echo=FALSE, results='asis', eval=has_gstat}
ok    <- is.finite(ka$se) & is.finite(ka$plain_var) & ka$plain_var > 0 &
         ka$n >= 2
ratio <- median(ka$se[ok]^2 / ka$plain_var[ok])
shift <- ka$kr_shift[is.finite(ka$kr_shift)]
naive <- if (ratio < 1) {
  sprintf("so the naive standard error is about %.0f percent too small",
          100 * (1 - sqrt(ratio)))
} else "so the naive standard error is not too small"
cat(sprintf(paste(
  "On this field the naive variance \\(s^2/n\\) is %.2f of `plain_var` in",
  "the median cell, %s for the cell's own mean. Kriging removes a median",
  "%.0f percent of the plain mean's error variance. `kr_shift` is beyond 1",
  "in %d of the %d cells and beyond 2 in %d, against about %.0f and %.0f",
  "for a right variogram, and the variance of the standardised errors is",
  "%.2f.\n"),
  ratio, naive, 100 * median(ka$kr_gain, na.rm = TRUE),
  sum(abs(shift) > 1), length(shift), sum(abs(shift) > 2),
  2 * pnorm(-1) * length(shift), 2 * pnorm(-2) * length(shift),
  attr(ka, "cv")$zscore_var))
```

```{r kriging-no-gstat, echo=FALSE, eval=!has_gstat, results='asis'}
cat("*(The kriging check needs `gstat`, which is not installed here.)*\n")
```

```{r se-empty, include=FALSE}
se_empty <- sum(!tess$cells$poly_id %in% asg$poly_id)
```

An empty cell still gets a kriged estimate and variance, and the `empty
cells` line of the report counts them. This grid of `r nrow(tess$cells)`
cells over `r nrow(asg)` points has
`r if (se_empty == 0) "none" else se_empty`.

## Pooled values and their warnings

`summarize_by_cell()` reports problems with the pooled values, and with
whether the cells match the count chosen for them, as R warnings with a
class. Each is raised once per call and reason and carries its numbers as
fields, so you can catch one by its class and read it without matching its
text; a warning about the pooled columns also names the columns it applies
to. `?"spatialkit-conditions"` lists every
class the package raises. The helper below runs a call and returns the
classes it raised:

```{r raised}
raised <- function(expr) {
  seen <- character(0)
  withCallingHandlers(expr, warning = function(w) seen <<- c(seen, class(w)[1]))
  seen
}
```

The Voronoi cells above were sized for pooled values at 4.5 observations
per cell. `select_resolution()` keeps a record of that
choice: the count, the rule that set it and the cell value it was chosen for.
The seeds, the cells and the assigned rows carry the record, and
`summarize_by_cell()` checks each summary against it. A summary of the value
the count was chosen for, on the cells and rows that were scored, raises
nothing:

```{r pooled-clean}
raised(summarize_by_cell(asg_v, "z", id_col = "cell_id", cells_sf = vor$cells))
```

Each warning below is a departure from that.

### The count was chosen for the other value (`spatialkit_estimate_mismatch`)

This call asks for plain means from cells whose count was set for pooled
values. `tryCatch()` catches the warning by its class, and the chunk prints
its text and its fields:

```{r mismatch}
w <- tryCatch(
  summarize_by_cell(asg_v, "z", id_col = "cell_id", cells_sf = vor$cells,
                    estimate = "mean"),
  spatialkit_estimate_mismatch = function(w) w)
writeLines(strwrap(conditionMessage(w), 76))
unlist(unclass(w)[c("chosen_for", "reported", "rule", "cells")])
```

The summary is returned as asked. Report the value the count was chosen for,
or choose the count for the value you report:
`resolution_profile(estimate = "mean")` with
`select_resolution(criterion = "loo")`.

### Not the cells and rows that were scored (`spatialkit_cells_differ`)

The summary fits the response again on what it is given and compares the
rows, the cells that hold one and the leave-one-out error with the record.
Here twenty rows are dropped after the assignment:

```{r differ}
w <- tryCatch(
  summarize_by_cell(asg_v[-(1:20), ], "z", id_col = "cell_id",
                    cells_sf = vor$cells),
  spatialkit_cells_differ = function(w) w)
writeLines(strwrap(conditionMessage(w), 76))
w$what
rbind(scored = unlist(w$scored), found = unlist(w$found))
```

`what` names the first comparison that failed: `"n"` for another number of
rows with a response, `"cells"` for another number of cells that hold one,
`"loo"` for the same rows in the same number of cells with another
leave-one-out error, which means rows sit in other cells, and `"record"` when
the assigned layer and `cells_sf` carry different records. The usual causes
are rows filtered after the assignment, a boundary that leaves points in no
cell, and a layer other than the one profiled. Points on a boundary between
two cells, as on gridded data, are placed so that a lattice passes the check;
`?summarize_by_cell` ("Value") lists the cases where they are not. The
returned values describe the cells as given, `attr(, "count_rule")$check`
keeps the outcome, and cells you bring yourself carry no record and are not
checked.

### No better than one mean (`spatialkit_no_structure`)

`b` is noise by construction. This chunk shows the warning as R prints it:

```{r no-structure, warning=TRUE}
noise <- summarize_by_cell(asg_v, "b", id_col = "cell_id")
as.data.frame(attr(noise, "pooled")$columns$resp_b[
  c("loo", "loo_one_cell", "structure_p", "own_weight", "structured")])
```

`structured` is `TRUE` only when one mean for all rows predicts a left-out
row more than 2 percent worse than the pooled values do (`loo_one_cell`
against `loo`) and the F test of the cell means against one mean gives a
p-value below 0.05 (`structure_p`). Otherwise it is `FALSE`, and the warning
is raised. The values are still returned, and a map of them looks smooth,
because each is mostly the mean of its neighbours. On 200 simulated layers
with white noise as the response, the median own weight was 0.11, and a
cell's pooled value had a correlation of 0.79 with the mean of the pooled
values of its 8 nearest cells, where the plain means had one of -0.02
([`dev/sim-pooled-values.R`](https://github.com/elkronos/gis_modeling_toolkit/blob/main/dev/sim-pooled-values.R)
in the package's GitHub repository; `?summarize_by_cell` gives the settings
under "How this was checked").

### Values with no pooling (`spatialkit_pool_degenerate`)

Its `reason` says which of three cases it is. A column that does not vary
inside any cell is one of them:

```{r degenerate}
asg_v$flat <- 1
w <- tryCatch(summarize_by_cell(asg_v, "flat", id_col = "cell_id"),
              spatialkit_pool_degenerate = function(w) w)
writeLines(strwrap(conditionMessage(w), 76))
w$reason
```

With `"no spread inside any cell"` and with `"one cell"`, every own weight is
1 and the pooled value is the plain mean. With `"no signal between cells"`,
the cell means differ from their targets by no more than the spread inside
the cells explains: every own weight is 0, and each pooled value is its
target and holds none of the cell's own observations.
`spatialkit_no_structure` is the warning that marks a response without
structure: in the simulation it was raised on all 200 white-noise layers, and
the reason `"no signal between cells"` on 20 of them.

### Too few cells for neighbours (`spatialkit_pool_few_cells`)

With 2 to 9 cells, the neighbours of a cell are all the other cells, so its
target is the mean of every observation outside it. A square grid asked for
very few cells shows it:

```{r few-cells, warning=TRUE}
few   <- build_tessellation(pts, boundary = bnd, method = "square",
                            approx_n_cells = 4, quiet = TRUE)$cells
asg_f <- assign_features_to_polygons(pts, few, quiet = TRUE)
four  <- summarize_by_cell(asg_f, "z")
round(as.data.frame(four)[, c("poly_id", "n", "resp_mean_z", "..pooled_resp_z",
                              "..pooled_w_resp_z", "..pooled_target_resp_z")],
      3)
```

The grid has `r nrow(few)` cells, and the cells numbered
`r paste(setdiff(few$poly_id, four$poly_id), collapse = " and ")`, strips at
the edge of the box, hold no point, so the summary has a row for each of the
other `r nrow(four)`. The overall mean lies between a cell's own mean and its
target. A cell whose own weight is below its share of the observations
therefore gets a pooled value on the far side of the overall mean from its
plain mean, and two cells can change order. The `..pooled_w_*` column shows
how close each cell is to that, and `estimate = "mean"` gives the plain means.

`?summarize_by_cell` lists these classes and the other warnings of the pooled
values under "Conditions", with the fields each carries.

## Values at other locations

`cell_values_at()` gives a location the value of the cell it lies in, the
pooled value when the summary holds one, and its distance from the nearest
observation. `dist_ratio` is that distance over the layer's spacing (the
median distance from an observation to the nearest other), the number to
report beside a value read anywhere but at an observation. Passing the seeds
the cells were built on, each with its cell from `vor$index`, extends each
Voronoi cell past the clipped edge, so a location outside every cell takes
the cell of its nearest seed. The third location below lies outside the
boundary:

```{r values-at}
seeds$cell_id <- vor$index
where <- st_as_sf(data.frame(x = 5e5 + c(250, 600, 1300),
                             y = 5e6 + c(250, 700, 500)),
                  coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632)
at <- cell_values_at(where, vals, asg_v, "z", id_col = "cell_id", seeds = seeds)
at[c("value", "dist_ratio")] <- lapply(at[c("value", "dist_ratio")], round, 2)
at[, c("cell_id", "value", "estimate", "filled", "dist_ratio")]
```

Without `seeds`, a location outside every cell comes back with
`filled = TRUE`, and `filled_from` names the cell its value was taken from.
`vignette("reporting")` shows the same call with intervals, and what to
report with them.
